Internal Assessment (l1A) 
You should be able to: 
v/ demonstrate knowledge and understanding 
v’ apply knowledge and understanding to 
specific situations and problems 
v analyse, evaluate and synthesize information 
v demonstrate the application of skills 
necessary to carry out insightful and ethical 
investigations. 
Internal assessment (IA) is an integral part of the 
IB Diploma Programme in Chemistry. IA is based on 
an individual investigation, for which you will need to 
choose a research question, develop a research design 
that would allow you to answer that question, carry out 
the investigation under your teacher's supervision and 
write a detailed report on your work. The main purpose 
of IAis the evaluation of your ability to carry out insightful 
and ethical investigations using the scientific method 
(figure 1). 
Assessment tip 
You are expected to spend approximately 10 hours on 
your investigation, although in some cases much more 
time may be required to complete all planned and 
unplanned tasks. The course, duration and outcome 
of any kind of scientific research are difficult to predict, 
so the earlier you begin your work, the better!

The IA contributes 20% to your final grade. Unlike 
examination papers, which are marked externally, the |A 
will be marked internally by your teacher and moderated 
externally by the IB at the end of the course. The 
assessment of your work will be based on your individual 
performance, and your final score will not be related to 
that of other students. 
Mark criteria 
Your investigation will be marked using the four 
criteria listed in Table 1. Each criterion contributes up 
to six marks (25%) to the total |A score of 24 marks. 
To maximize your score, it is important to understand 
these criteria and the way your work will be evaluated 
by your teacher. 
Assessment tip 
Understanding the mark criteria will help you to 
maximize your |A score. 
Criterion Maximum mark 
Research design 6

A Table 1 Mark criteria for the IA 
Research design assesses your ability to describe the 
methodology of your research, including the purpose 
of your research question and the practical approaches 
used in your work to address that question. The research 
question must be meaningful, focused and unambiguous. 
The context of the research question should include a 
reference to the dependent and independent variables, 
or two correlated variables, that will be studied in your 
work. You must also provide a brief description of the 
system to which the research question is applied, and 
include a background theory that is relevant to the 
question and its context.

Internal Assessment (1A) 
Your description of the research methodology should 
cover the following points: 
* model(s) or database(s) used in your investigation 
(if applicable) 
* methods used for measuring the dependent and 
independent variables 
* the scope, quantity and quality of the measurements 
* the choice of control variables 
» safety, ethical and/or environmental considerations. 
The research methodology must be presented concisely, 
without unnecessary repetitions or irrelevant information. 
At the same time, your report must contain sufficient 
detail to allow any other researcher to understand your 
methodology and repeat your investigation. 
Data analysis assesses your ability to record, process and 
present the quantitative and gualitative data relevant to 
the research question. To score the maximum mark on 
this criterion, your report must show that all experimental 
data are: 
* relevantto the research question 
* recorded ina clear and precise manner 
* processed with appropriate consideration of 
uncertainties. 
The methods of data processing should be easily 
understood by any other researcher, and the presented 
results should follow the conventions adopted by the 
scientific community, including appropriate referencing, 
annotation of graphs and tables, and the use of units, 
decimal places and significant figures. Remember that 
any omissions, inaccuracies or inconsistencies in the 
recorded and processed data will have a negative impact 
on your ability to draw valid conclusions that address the 
research guestion. 
Conclusion assesses your ability to answer the research 
question by analysing the data acquired during your 
experimental or theoretical studies and with regard to 
the accepted scientific context. This criterion also takes 
into account your interpretation of the experimental 
results, including uncertainties, and the way you use 
the information from scientific papers, textbooks or 
online resources, including correct and sufficiently 
detailed references to any material that is not your 
own work. 
230 
Evaluation assesses the extent to which your report 
evaluates the methodology of your investigation and 
suggests realistic improvements that address specific 
methodological weaknesses or limitations. Potential 
weaknesses could include the control of variables, 
accuracy and precision of measurements or the degree 
of natural variation of the collected data. Limitations 
may include the range of collected data, constraints 
of the system and the effects of various assumptions 
you have made. To score the maximum mark, you 
are expected to estimate the relative impact of these 
weaknesses and limitations on the outcome of your 
investigation and explain why the improvements you 
have suggested are relevant to any identified issues. 
Assessment tip 
After every examination session, the IB publishes 
a subject report for Chemistry. Before you embark 
on your investigation, read the latest subject 
report. In particular, look at the recommendations 
from the Chief Moderator and the analysis of the 
strengths and weaknesses of the candidates. 
By doing this, you will learn about typical issues 
found in other students’ reports and gain a better 
understanding of how your own work will be 
marked and moderated. By following the best 
practices and avoiding common pitfalls, you will 
not only maximize your score but will also improve 
your research, analytical and presentation skills, 
which will ultimately give you a solid head start in 
your future career. 
Referencing and academic integrity 
As was mentioned earlier, you are expected to provide 
appropriate referencing to any sourced information 
used in your report. Although the exact style of 
referencing or in-text citation is not specified, it must 
be consistent throughout your work and include the 
following information: 
¢ author name(s) 
* publication date 
* original title 
* page number(s) for scientific papers or books 
* link and access date for online materials.

Internal Assessment (IA) 
In your |A report, you must clearly distinguish between 
your own words and those of others by the use of 
quotation marks followed by an appropriate citation. Any 
graphs, images or data published in print or in electronic 
sources must also be referenced. 
All coursewark, including IA, must be authentic, based 
on your own ideas and analysis. When collaborative 
work is involved, your report must clearly show 
your individual contribution to the investigation 
and acknowledge the experimental data, analytical 
results or any other information provided by other 
students. Failure to acknowledge the work of others is 
academic malpractice, which will significantly impact 
your |A score and, in extreme cases, lead to a penalty 
imposed by the IB. 
Choice of research question 
and design 
The first decision you will have to make is what to 
research, how and why. You will also have to decide how 
to collect data to answer the research question; this can 
include laboratory experiments and/or use of databases 
and computer modelling. An interesting research 
question that yields little data, or data of limited scope 
and/or relevance, will score very poorly. In many cases, 
you will need to try out several ideas before you embark 
on a full investigation. 
Assessment tips 
Communicate your interest in the investigation and 
pose a guestion to which you do not already know the 
answer. Try to design an original method or apply a 
known technique to an interesting or unusual real￾world situation. 
Do not use a known method without any 
modifications. Explain why a particular method is 
suitable for your investigation and give a reason for 
any modification you make. 
The research question must be specific and 
unambiguous. For example, the question “Investigating 
enthalpies of combustion” is too vague and thus not 
acceptable for the IA. In contrast, the question “The 
effect of isomerism on the enthalpy of combustion of 
saturated alcohols” is appropriate, although it could be 
improved further by specifying the range of alcohols used 
in your investigation. 
Assessment tip 
Try to develop a question that does not have an 
obvious outcome, such as determining how the 
mass of a combusted alcohol affects the amount of 
heat produced. Also, avoid questions involving the 
comparison of commercial products, as any differences 
or trends identified in your study might reflect business￾related decisions rather than scientific principles. 
A good research question will allow you to determine a 
relationship between a continuous independent variable, 
such as concentration or temperature, and a dependent 
variable that can be measured precisely in a school 
laboratory. Dependent variables can include volume 
of gas or titrant, mass of precipitate, reaction rate or 
thermochemical data. To clarify your ideas, you can put all 
the information together using table 2 as a template.

Any investigation should generate sufficient experimental 
data, which must be suitable for processing and analysis. 
To estimate the amount of data you need, look at data￾based questions from past examination papers. 
Assessment tip 
Failure to identify a suitable independent variable 
or generate usable data will limit the scope and 
depth of your investigation and therefore make it 
less successful. 
231

Internal Assessment (1A) 
In most cases, you will need to collect primary data 
yourself, although the use of databases and simulations is 
also possible. Many experimental measurements can be 
carried out using the most basic instruments available in a 
school laboratory. However, you should always consider 
the use of more sophisticated equipment, such as digital 
sensors or data-loggers. Alternatively, you can easily 
turn your mobile phone into a data-logger by making a 
video recording of your experiments and processing the 
recorded information, for example, instrument readings 
at regular time intervals. 
You should also estimate the number of measurements 
required for making a meaningful and justified conclusion. 
Run several trials to make sure that you can generate a 
sufficient amount of useful data. If this is not the case, alter 
your methodology until you are satisfied with the results 
of your preliminary studies. 
Assessment tip 
The rule of thumb is to carry out three or more trials of 
each experiment and record five or more values of the 
independent variable in each trial. 
If you use secondary data, or data from models and 
simulations, you will need to include several databases 
or models in your research. By doing so, you will not only 
increase the initial set of data available for analysis but also 
extend the scope of your investigation by enabling the 
evaluation of data variance between the sources. 
After formulating the research question, you will need to 
provide relevant background information, which should 
focus on the specifics of your research methodology. 
In particular, you should describe the context for your 
research question, summarize the existing knowledge 
and provide balanced chemical equations for the key 
reactions used in your investigation. 
Choose equipment that will allow you to collect reliable 
data. For example, consider using volumetric glassware 
rather than graduated cylinders for measuring volumes. 
Include a section in your report to provide a detailed 
description of the apparatus and materials used in your 
investigation. 
232 
Assessment tip 
Use the most precise apparatus available in your 
laboratory and state the precision of any equipment 
you use in your investigation. For example, state 
“25.0cm? =+ 0.1 cm? volumetric pipette” rather than 
“analytical pipette” or “pipette”. 
Make sure that your method is written in sufficient detail 
for any reader to repeat the investigation and estimate 
the associated uncertainties. Consider describing briefly 
the process of developing your methodology, which will 
provide insight into your decision-making skills. 
Finally, include a section about the safety, ethical and 
environmental issues relevant to your research. This 
section might be very basic, such as noting the need 
for personal protective equipment while working 
in the laboratory, but it could also cover safe and 
environmentally responsible disposal of reagents, 
recovery and reuse of solvents, or application of “green 
chemistry” techniques. 
Assessment tip 
Typical layout of the “Research design” section of 
your report: 
* research question 
* background information 
* variables 
* apparatus 
* method 
* safety

Internal Assessment (IA) 
Data analysis 
In this section of your report, you need to demonstrate 
that you have selected, recorded, processed and 
interpreted the data in ways that are relevant to the 
research question and can support the conclusion of 
your investigation. 
To achieve a high score, follow the recommendations 
listed below. 
1. Collect enough data for meaningful processing and 
interpretation. The data must include independent 
and dependent variables, control variables and

In addition to these recommendations, make sure that 
you report only data and observations in this section, not 
inferences. For example, the rates of a given reaction with 
and without a catalyst are the data while the conclusion that 
the catalyst increases the reaction rate is an inference. Any 
inferences should be made in the “Conclusion” section.

Report both raw and processed data. For example, 
provide the volume of titrant used in each repeated 
measurement together with the average volume rather 
than the average volume only. 
If necessary, use photographs to support your data 
but never replace data with photographs or images. 
Produce well-designed tables that enable comparison 
of data and contain all the necessary information, 
including descriptive titles, labelled columns and 
rows, correct symbols and units for physical quantities, 
and uncertainties of experimental data. 
. Draw all graphs to scale, provide descriptive titles 
and label all axes with the correct symbols, units and 
multiplication factors (if applicable). Use best-fit lines 
or curves where appropriate. 
. Show your processing clearly, but do not add 
unnecessary steps and descriptions. Provide sample 
calculations for key processing steps but do not 
include calculations of repeating data. 
Use scientific notation for very small or very large 
values, and round all intermediate and final results to 
the correct number of significant figures or decimal 
places. Use a consistent format for each type of data. 
. Estimate the precision of your data from the results of 
repeated measurements and technical specifications 
of the instruments used in your research. Estimate the 
accuracy of your measurements by comparing your 
results with literature values or theoretical predictions.

Internal Assessment (1A) 
Conclusion 
At the end of your report, you will have to present a 
conclusion that is relevant to the research question 
and justified by the data within a specific scientific 
context. This conclusion can be formulated in many 
ways, although in most cases you will need to produce 
a graph or plot that shows the relationship between the 
independent and dependent variables, and explain the 
meaning and significance of that relationship. The graph 
or plot should satisfy the general requirements outlined 
in Tool 3.4. The quality of a linear fit should be analysed 
using statistical methods, including the calculation of the 
R?value for the best-it line. The sources and significance 
of any outliers should be discussed in your report, 
and their exclusion from statistical processing should 
be justified. 
Assessment tip 
Make sure that the type of graph or plot you use 
matches the type of data. For more detail, see 
Tool 3.4. 
You will also need to demonstrate how the results of 
your investigation are related to the accepted scientific 
context, such as published experimental data or common 
trends described in textbooks and research papers. 
Any sourced information used in your report must be 
referenced clearly and consistently. 
Evaluation 
The evaluation part of your report should include two 
main components: 
¢ critical review of the methodology used in your 
investigation 
* suggestions of how this methodology could be 
improved. 
The critical discussion can cover any issues related to 
your experimental data and their evaluation, such as the 
accuracy and precision of measurements, the sources 
and effects of systematic and random errors, the range 
of data collected and the use of control variables. You 
can also discuss the validity of your methodology and 
conclusion in terms of the accepted scientific context by 
comparing your experimental results with literature data. 
However, any significant mistakes in methodology will 
234 
affect your score towards the “Research design” criterion, 
so identifying such mistakes at this stage will earn you 
minimal credit. 
Any improvements you suggest must be realistic and 
relevant. In other words, you must take into account safety 
issues, the cost and availability of equipment, the time 
required for additional experiments, and the expected 
effect of each improvement on the quality and validity of 
collected data. In all cases, any suggested improvements 
must address the methodological weaknesses or 
limitations of your investigation identified earlier. 
Assessment tip 
Avoid making obvious or general suggestions, such 
as “doing more trials” or “using a better balance”, 
without detailed analysis of their effects on the 
experimental results. 
Finally, you may want to discuss briefly any possible 
extensions to your investigation, which should also be 
realistic and scientifically justified. 
General advice 
It is essential to demonstrate your ability to communicate 
scientific knowledge effectively. Make sure that your 
report is written clearly and formatted correctly, and 
that it meets all formal requirements for the |A, including 
the structure and length. Do not include too much 
background information; instead, focus on the research 
question. Describe your methodology in sufficient detail 
and include worked examples of calculations. Provide 
citations and references for anything that is not your 
own work. Do not waste space by including unnecessary 
pictures of chemicals and standard equipment, such as 
laboratory glassware or analytical instruments. Avoid 
providing extra information in an appendix, as it will 
not be assessed. Double-check all calculations and 
make sure that you have labelled all axes in the graphs, 
included units in data tables and used an appropriate 
number of significant figures and decimal places in all 
numerical values. 
Finally, good luck!
